pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Invasive Species (ages 9–11): non-native animals (or plants) introduced by humans to places they don't naturally belong, which harm native wildlife by outcompeting for food, spreading disease, or having no natural predators to keep them in check.
• Standards — UK (DfE): enriches Y4 'Living things and their habitats' (interdependence; environments can change) and Y6 adaptation; a human-impact case within ecology.
• Standards — US (NGSS): MS-LS2-4 (changes to an ecosystem's physical/biological components affect populations); MS-LS2-1 (resource availability affects organisms/populations); builds on 3-LS4-3.
• Operational details: define invasive vs merely non-native (an introduced species becomes invasive when it spreads and causes harm). Anchor with examples — grey squirrels outcompeting UK red squirrels (and carrying squirrelpox), cane toads poisoning Australian predators, European rabbits devastating Australian vegetation, lionfish in the Atlantic, Burmese pythons in the Everglades. Explain WHY invasives succeed: released from their native predators/parasites, they breed unchecked and outcompete or prey on natives that never evolved defences against them. Distinguish human introduction from a species naturally expanding its range.
• Checkpoint — A (concrete, ~9): define invasive species and give an example and its impact. B (transitional, ~10): give at least 2 reasons invasives are harmful (no predators, outcompete, disease). C (formal, ~11): distinguish a human-introduced invasive from natural range expansion, and explain why native species often can't cope.
bestPractices: Build the concept from the mechanism 'no natural enemies here', running the logic that a species freed from its home predators/parasites can multiply and dominate.
Use paired native-vs-invasive cases (red vs grey squirrel) so pupils see the DIRECT harm — competition, disease — not just 'a new animal arrived'.
Explicitly separate 'non-native' from 'invasive' and 'natural range shift' from 'human introduction', since the harm and the human role are what define the concept.
Connect to natural selection: natives lack evolved defences against a novel enemy because they never faced it — tying back to adaptation over generations.
keyRepresentations: A before/after ecosystem diagram: native community, then an invasive added, with population arrows showing natives crashing.
A paired comparison card (red vs grey squirrel) listing competition and disease impacts.
A 'released from control' diagram: the species with its native predators vs the same species with none in the new place.
A map showing human-mediated introduction routes (trade, pets, ballast water).
commonMisconceptions: 'Any non-native animal is invasive' — only introduced species that spread and cause harm are invasive.
'Invasive species are naturally evil / more aggressive by nature' — they thrive largely because they lack the predators/parasites that controlled them at home.
'The animals invaded on purpose' — most were moved by humans (trade, pets, stowaways), not by their own choice.
'A species moving into a new area naturally is invasive' — natural range expansion is different from human-introduced invasion.
'Introducing another animal to eat the invasive always fixes it' — biological control can itself become a new invasive disaster (e.g. cane toads introduced to control beetles).

learn.summary: Invasive species (ages 9–11): non-native animals or plants moved by humans to places they don't naturally belong, which harm native wildlife by outcompeting for food, spreading disease, or thriving because no local predators or parasites keep them in check. Learners build the concept from the mechanism 'released from natural control' rather than 'the invader is a stronger/better animal', using paired native-vs-invasive cases and distinguishing human introduction from natural range expansion. A population-dynamics simulation is the recommended lead activity, with categorisation/matching to assess the distinctions and a management-dilemma discussion as an optional extension.

activities.title: Introduce a species: a population-dynamics simulation
feedback: If a learner says the invader 'won because it's stronger', prompt: run the same species WITH its home predators present. If adding its old predators changes the outcome, then being 'stronger' cannot be the whole explanation, and the missing controls matter too. Some invaders also have particular advantages (such as carrying a disease), but the missing controls are a key part of the cause.

When the control toggle is OFF and native meters crash, highlight: in this model, the only thing that changed was the absence of predators/parasites. That is the mechanism this run isolates, though real ecosystems involve more factors.

For the route selector, point out that the species does not behave differently because of how it arrived; what changes is the classification. 'Invasive' requires human introduction and harm, so being somewhere new is not by itself the same as being invasive.
After the cane-toad scenario, draw out: a quick fix that adds another species can create a worse problem than the one it was meant to solve.
activities.rationale: Population interaction and causal reasoning are made visible when a learner can change one variable (presence of home predators/parasites) and watch native populations respond; this is intended to address the 'stronger/better animal' misconception by relocating the cause to the new environment. Toggle, meter and route-selector examples are offered as illustrations of the mechanism, not as a mandatory interface, and the activity is a research-informed proposal rather than a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: An introduced species becomes invasive when it spreads and harms native wildlife; invasives often thrive because they are released from the natural predators/parasites that controlled them in their native range.
Changes to an ecosystem's components and resource availability affect populations of organisms.
learnerActions: Start with a balanced native ecosystem shown with live population meters for the native species.
Drop in a non-native animal and watch what happens to the meters over time.
Toggle whether the predators and parasites that controlled the newcomer in its home range are present or absent, and compare the two outcomes.
Predict before each run whether native populations will crash or settle, then check against the meters.
State in your own words why native populations crashed in the simulation runs where the invader's home predators were absent.

Use a route selector to show the animal arriving via human trade or as an escaped pet, versus a species slowly walking into new territory on its own, and discuss how each would be classified. The animal's biology is the same either way; what differs is whether humans moved it.
Run a 'biological control backfires' scenario: release a species to fix one problem (e.g. cane toads to eat beetles) and observe it becoming a second invasive.
activities.intendedInsight: The damage an invasive causes is not because it is 'evil' or inherently superior; the main mechanism this simulation shows is that nothing in the new place keeps it in check and native species never evolved defences against it, with competition and specific advantages like disease adding to the harm in particular cases. Human introduction and the resulting harm are what define 'invasive', distinct from natural range expansion.

activities.title: Red vs grey: paired native/invasive comparison
feedback: If a learner only notes 'a new animal is there', ask them to name the exact mechanism of harm for that pair (e.g. greys carry squirrelpox that kills reds).

Reinforce that in their own native range in North America, grey squirrels are perfectly ordinary. The harm in the UK comes from them being out of place, where they carry squirrelpox and compete with red squirrels that never evolved alongside them.
activities.rationale: Paired native-vs-invasive cases make the direct harm concrete and are proposed to counter the vague 'an animal moved in' reading. Before/after diagrams and comparison cards are offered as supporting fixed representations, not required media.
sourceClaims: Grey squirrels outcompete UK red squirrels and carry squirrelpox; cane toads introduced to Australia poison native predators; these are canonical invasive-species cases.

An introduced species becomes invasive when it spreads and harms native wildlife; invasives often thrive because they are released from the natural predators/parasites that controlled them in their native range.
learnerActions: Study a before/after picture of a native community, then the same community after an invasive is added, with arrows showing native populations declining.
Fill in a paired comparison card for red squirrel vs grey squirrel, listing the specific harms: competition for food and squirrelpox disease (deadly to reds, not to greys).

Add at least one more canonical case and its impact, choosing from: cane toads poisoning Australian predators, European rabbits devastating Australian vegetation, lionfish in the Atlantic, or Burmese pythons in the Everglades.
Explain, for each case, whether the harm comes mainly from competition, disease, lack of predators, or predation on natives that lack defences.
activities.intendedInsight: Invasives cause specific, identifiable harms (competition, disease, unchecked predation) to native species — 'a new animal arrived' is not the whole story; the harm is the defining feature.

activities.title: Sort and match: native, non-native, invasive
feedback: If a learner labels any non-native animal 'invasive', remind them harm and spread are required, not just being from elsewhere.
If a learner calls a native wasp or fierce native predator 'invasive', point out a native species cannot be invasive however dangerous it is.
If a learner labels the climate-driven bird 'invasive', contrast natural range shift with human introduction. Under the definition used here, the human role and the harm are what define the term.
activities.rationale: Categorisation and matching can assess the distinctions and surface misconceptions such as 'any non-native = invasive' and 'they invaded on purpose'. Sorting consolidates and checks the category distinctions but does not itself display the population dynamics, so it works best alongside the simulation.
sourceClaims: An introduced species becomes invasive when it spreads and harms native wildlife; invasives often thrive because they are released from the natural predators/parasites that controlled them in their native range.
learnerActions: Sort a set of species into three categories: native, non-native but harmless, and invasive (non-native, human-introduced, and causing harm).
Match each invasive species to its main impact (e.g. grey squirrel → squirrelpox and competition; cane toad → poisoning predators).
Decide for each scenario whether it describes a human introduction or a natural range expansion, and justify the choice.
Answer: a bird slowly spreads north on its own as the climate warms — is that invasive? Explain why or why not.
activities.intendedInsight: Invasive is a precise category: non-native AND introduced by humans AND causing harm; a native pest is not invasive, and a species naturally extending its range is not automatically invasive.

activities.title: Ranger's dilemma: how do we control an invasive without making it worse? (optional)
feedback: If a learner proposes adding a predator to eat the invasive, ask what controls THAT predator in its new home — the cane toad shows an introduced control can become the next disaster.
Steer discussion back to the underlying mechanism: a lasting fix must account for the absence of natural controls, not just add another species.
activities.rationale: A role-play discussion is a motivating hook for the management dilemma and connects the mechanism to real decisions; it is offered as an extension, since the population dynamics are proposed to be shown more directly through the simulation in this design. A discussion can rehearse reasoning but does not itself display the dynamics.
learnerActions: Take on the role of an ecologist or ranger discussing a real management problem for a chosen invasive.
Propose how you might reduce the invasive's impact, then consider what could go wrong with each idea.
Use the cane toad case to argue why adding a new predator or control species can itself become a new invasion.
Distinguish, in discussion, which harms come from competition, disease, or absence of predators, and how that affects what management might work.
activities.intendedInsight: Managing invasives is a reasoning problem with trade-offs; introducing another species as a 'fix' can backfire, as the cane toad case shows.

constraints: Distinguish 'non-native' from 'invasive': an introduced species becomes invasive only when it spreads AND causes harm.
Distinguish human introduction (trade, pets, stowaways/ballast water) from a species naturally expanding its range; both the human role and the harm are part of the definition.

Locate the cause of harm in the new environment (no predators/parasites/competitors to keep the species in check, plus specific advantages like disease), not in the invader being inherently 'stronger', 'better', or 'evil'.
Native species cannot be invasive, however much of a pest or however dangerous they are.
Biological control is not a guaranteed safe fix — a released control species can itself become a worse invasive (cane toad example).
Sort/match tasks assess the category distinctions but do not by themselves make the population dynamics visible; pair them with the simulation.

Before/after diagrams and comparison cards are fixed representations: they can illustrate the harm but cannot be manipulated to test 'what if the predators were present', which is the observable affordance the simulation adds; this is not a claim that other media cannot teach the concept.
Connect to adaptation/natural selection where appropriate: natives lack evolved defences against a novel enemy because they never faced it over generations.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; all sources[].verified were false in the original and have NOT been re-checked. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original rated a 3D interactive as 'poor' claiming 'a 3D world adds nothing to the mechanism'; this universal comparative claim is not established by the source evidence and has been omitted rather than asserted. The 2D simulation is proposed for its ability to show population changes and toggle one variable, not as proof that other media cannot teach the concept.

The original quiz rationale said categorisation/matching 'test rather than reveal the dynamics' — retained as a scoped limitation (recognition/sorting consolidates distinctions but does not itself display dynamics), not as a universal law that quizzes only assess.

Whether 'release from natural control' is the single dominant cause or one contributor alongside competition and disease is not independently established; the lead activity's insight now frames enemy-release as the primary mechanism the simulation demonstrates while naming competition and disease as case-specific additions.

Squirrelpox being deadly to red squirrels but not grey squirrels, and cane toads being introduced to control beetles, are drawn from the source examples; biological/epidemiological specifics were not re-verified here.
The diagnostic 'correctAnswer' notes squirrelpox is deadly to reds but not greys and that greys also outcompete reds for food; these align with the source claims but remain unverified.
Efficacy comparisons between the simulation and other media are presented as proposed/intended wording because no empirical effectiveness evidence was supplied.

probeDeeper: Back in North America, are grey squirrels a problem? Why are they harmful in Britain but not there?
Is every animal that isn't native automatically invasive? What has to be true for 'invasive'?
A bird slowly spreads north on its own as the climate warms. Is that an invasive species? Why or why not?
Australia introduced cane toads to eat beetles. What went wrong, and what does it teach us?
assess.correctAnswer: 'Stronger and better' isn't the real reason. Grey squirrels thrive in Britain mainly because they are out of their natural place — the predators, competitors and diseases that would keep them in check back home aren't here. They also outcompete reds for food and carry a virus (squirrelpox) that is deadly to reds but not to them. So the harm comes from being introduced somewhere with no natural controls, plus specific advantages like disease — not from being an all-round 'better' animal. In their native range, greys are perfectly ordinary.

errorPatterns.pattern: Invasive species take over because they're just stronger or better animals
errorPatterns.nextMove: Locate the cause in the new environment — no natural predators, competitors or diseases to keep them in check; in their native range they're ordinary.
errorPatterns.distractor: The grey squirrels took over because they're simply stronger, better animals than the reds.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes dominance to the species being tougher or better overall.

errorPatterns.pattern: Any animal that's a pest or dangerous is an invasive species
errorPatterns.nextMove: Define invasive precisely — non-native AND introduced by humans AND causing harm; a native pest is not invasive.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls a native wasp or a fierce native predator 'invasive'.

errorPatterns.pattern: A species moving into a new area on its own is the same as being invasive
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast natural range shifts with human-introduced species; the human introduction and the rapid harm are what define 'invasive'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels a bird naturally extending its range as invasive.

errorPatterns.pattern: Introducing a new predator to control a pest is a safe fix
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the cane toad — introduced to control beetles, it became a worse invasive, poisoning native predators; introductions often backfire.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Proposes adding a predator without foreseeing it becoming invasive itself.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks 'invasive' means any pest or dangerous animal, or that invasives dominate because they're inherently stronger; can't separate natural spread from human introduction.
responseLevels.full: Defines invasive as non-native, human-introduced and harmful; gives examples with impacts; explains the harm through absence of natural predators/controls, competition and disease rather than inherent superiority; and distinguishes human introduction from natural range expansion.
responseLevels.partial: Defines invasive and gives an example with an impact, but explains the harm loosely — defaulting to 'stronger' rather than lack of natural controls — or blurs natural range expansion with human introduction.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Grey squirrels, brought to Britain from North America, have pushed out the native red squirrels. A student says the greys took over 'because they're just stronger, better animals.' Is that the real reason — or is something else going on?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the 'stronger/better animal' idea explains dominance by inherent superiority. A child who understands cites the absence of natural predators and controls in the new place, competition, and disease. Locating the cause in being out-of-place rather than superiority is the discriminator.
